'''''Apium graveolens''''', commonly known as '''celery''',<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020>{{cite web |title=Wild Celery ''Apium graveolens'' L. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P. A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R. J. Burkmar |editor4=O. L. Pescott |editor5=D. B. Roy |editor6=K. J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.v7h |access-date=2 September 2024 }}</ref><ref name = Streeter>Streeter D, Hart-Davies C, Hardcastle A, Cole F, Harper L. 2009. ''Collins Flower Guide''. Harper Collins {{ISBN|9-78-000718389-0 }}</ref> is an Old World species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Apiaceae]]. It was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.

The species is widely [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] outside of its natural range and is used as a vegetable; modern [[cultivar]]s have been selected for their leaf stalks ([[celery]]), a large bulb-like hypocotyl ([[celeriac]]), and their leaves ([[leaf celery]]).

==Description==
''Apium graveolens'' is a stout [[biennial plant|biennial]] or [[monocarpic]] perennial herb, producing flowers and seeds only once, during its second or a later year.<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020/> It grows up to {{cvt|1|m|ft|0}} tall, with all parts of the plant having a strong celery odour. The stems are solid with conspicuous grooves on the surface (sulcate). The [[leaves]] are bright green to yellowish-green, 1- to 2-[[pinnation|pinnate]] with leaflets that are variously shaped, often rhomboid, up to {{cvt|6|cm|frac=2}} long and {{cvt|4|cm|frac=2}} broad.

The flowers are produced in [[umbel]]s, mostly with short [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]], with four to twelve rays. The individual flowers are creamy-white to greenish-white, {{cvt|2|–|3|mm|in|frac=32}} across. The fruit is a [[schizocarp]], broadly ovoid to globose, {{cvt|1|–|1.5|mm|in|frac=64}} long and wide.<ref name="Streeter" /><ref name="blamey">Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}{{Page needed|date=July 2025 }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The species ''Apium graveolens'' was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.<ref name=IPNI_838067-1/> A large number of varieties have been described, none of which are accepted by [[Plants of the World Online]] {{As of|2024|May|lc=yes}}.<ref name=POWO_838067-1/> It has been selected as the [[type species]] of the genus ''[[Apium]]'', and through that, of the family [[Apiaceae]] and the order [[Apiales]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hitchcock |first1=A. S. |last2=Green |first2=M. L. |title=International Botanical Congress, Cambridge (England) 1930 |publisher=Printed under the authority of His Majesty's Stationery Office, by Wyman & sons, Ltd., Fetter Lane, London |location=London |date=1929 |page=142 |chapter=IV.-Proposal by A.S. Hitchcock (Washington) and M.L. Green (Kew). |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/viewer/13040/?offset=#page=143&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q= }}</ref>

The [[cultivar group]]s have often been given botanical variety names, but more accurately cultivar group names under the [[International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants]]. Thus cultivated celery was often called ''Apium graveolens'' var. ''dulce'',<ref name=RHS_Celery/> but as cultivated plants, ''Apium graveolens'' Dulce Group.<ref name=NCBI_Celery/>

Other vernacular names have been used, including "smallage", which is mostly archaic but still in occasional use, primarily outside of the species' native range.<ref name="OED">{{cite book |title=Oxford English Dictionary |date=1884 |publisher=Oxford University Press |page=Si-St 257 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Definition of 'smallage' |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/us/dictionary/english/smallage |website=Collins Dictionary }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Wild celery is [[Native species|native]] to much of Eurasia, ranging from Ireland in the west, through Europe north to Scotland, Denmark and Poland, and east to the [[Caucasus]] and Central Asia, and as far as the western [[Himalayas]], and also through [[Macaronesia]] and North Africa to West Asia and the [[Arabian Peninsula]].<ref name=POWO_838067-1/> It is widely [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] outside this range, including in Scandinavia, North and South America, Africa, India, central, eastern and southern Asia, and New Zealand.<ref name="POWO_838067-1" /> The cultivar groups may also be naturalised.<ref name="FE" />

It is a plant of damp places, usually near the coast where the soil is salty, typically on the brackish reaches of tidal rivers, ditch and dyke margins, saltmarshes, and sea walls.<ref name="BSBI_Atlas2020" /><ref name="Streeter" /><ref name="blamey" /><ref name="FE" /><ref name="Oberdorfer2001" /> North of the Alps, wild celery is found only in the foothill zone on soils with some salt content.<ref name="ExFlora" />

==Uses==
Wild celery was used for its medical properties and as a [[condiment]] by the Ancient Egyptians, Greeks and Romans, and also in China. The species was later developed as a vegetable, particularly in Italy from the 16th century. Modern [[cultivar]]s have been selected for different uses, falling into three groups according to the part that is mainly eaten:<ref name=Vilmorin/>
*[[Celery]] (''Apium graveolens'' Dulce Group; syn. ''Apium graveolens'' var. ''dulce''),<ref name=NCBI_Celery/> is used for its leaf stalks, which may be eaten raw or cooked.<ref name=RHS_Celery/>
*[[Celeriac]] (''Apium graveolens'' Rapaceum Group; syn. ''Apium graveolens'' var. ''rapaceum''),<ref name=NCBI_Celeriac/> is used for its swollen bulb-like [[hypocotyl]].<ref name=RHS_Celeriac/>
*[[Leaf celery]], smallage<ref name=NCEG/> or parcel (''Apium graveolens'' Secalinum Group; syn. ''Apium graveolens'' var. ''secalinum''),<ref name=NCBI_Leafcelery/> has larger leaves; both the leaves and stems are eaten.<ref name=RHS_Leafcelery/>
